content: 1. The search strategy included terms related to low-density lipoprotein (LDL), high-density lipoprotein (HDL), and lipoproteins in general, combined with terms for randomized controlled trials, clinical trials, placebo, drug therapy, and trial groups. These terms were used to identify relevant studies. 2. Medical Subject Headings (MeSH) descriptors were utilized to search for studies related to blood pressure, hypertension, potassium, potassium chloride, diet, norepinephrine, cholesterol, and triglycerides. Each descriptor was set to explode all trees to include all related subcategories. 3. Terms such as dietary, intake, reduction, and restriction did not retrieve MeSH terms. Similarly, terms like noradrenaline, catecholamine, low-density lipoprotein, and high-density lipoprotein also failed to retrieve MeSH terms. 4. A specific search was conducted to identify cohort studies involving children. Out of the results, 35 studies were found to include children or adolescents. Additional electronic searches were performed in EMBASE and Medline databases. 5. The PubMed search was conducted without language restrictions on September 21, 2011, and included studies published within the previous 180 days. The search combined terms for blood pressure, hypertension, potassium, potassium chloride, diet, dietary intake, restriction, and reduction, excluding animal studies. 6. Data extraction was performed using an Excel workbook divided into worksheets by topic area. Examples of worksheets included reference data, risk of bias information, study design, participant characteristics, and outcomes measured. 7. Risk of bias was assessed for various factors, including random sequence generation, allocation concealment, blinding, incomplete outcome data, selective reporting, and other potential sources of bias. Each trial was evaluated for systematic differences in care. 8. Participant characteristics were categorized by age group, sex, dietary interventions, and potassium intake levels. Subgroup analyses were performed based on hypertensive and normotensive status, as well as intervention and control group comparisons. 9. Outcomes measured included systolic and diastolic blood pressure, cholesterol levels, triglycerides, HDL, and LDL. Potassium intake at baseline and follow-up was also recorded, along with sodium intake and the duration of follow-up. 10. The research question focused on the effect of increased potassium intake compared to lower or usual potassium intake in children. The primary outcome was blood pressure, measured in mmHg, with lower values indicating better outcomes. 11. The quality of evidence was assessed using the GRADE framework, considering factors such as risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision, and other considerations. Serious risk of bias and imprecision were noted in some studies. 12. References included systematic reviews, meta-analyses, and individual studies on the relationship between potassium intake, blood pressure, and cardiovascular outcomes in both children and adults. These references provided a comprehensive overview of the evidence base.
